title: Ginger and Matcha Custard Ice Cream
changes_from_base: Matcha whisked into the milk and fresh ginger steeped in the dairy instead of vanilla.
summary: The classic French custard, flavoured with matcha whisked into the milk and fresh ginger steeped in the warm dairy instead of vanilla. Grassy, gently spicy and a lovely pale green.

ingredients.item: fresh ginger, finely grated with its juice
fine sea salt or table salt

steps.title: Whisk the matcha
steps.text: Sift the matcha into the saucepan and add the milk a splash at a time, whisking until completely smooth, then whisk in the cream. Matcha lumps will not dissolve later, so patience here pays off.

steps.title: Steep the ginger
steps.text: Heat until steaming, stir in the grated ginger with its juice, cover and leave off the heat for 45 min. Warm fat pulls the ginger's aromatic oils into the base.

steps.title: Beat the yolks
steps.text: In the heatproof bowl, whisk the yolks with the sugar until thick and pale. The mixture is stiff at first but loosens as you work it.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Rewarm the green dairy until steaming, whisk two ladles into the yolks and pour back into the pan.

steps.title: Cook gently
steps.text: Stir over low heat, scraping the base, until it coats the spatula and reads 77-80 °C. Overheating dulls matcha's colour, so stop as soon as it is there.

steps.title: Strain and chill
steps.text: Stir in the salt, then sieve, pressing on the ginger to extract its juice. Cool over the iced water and chill for at least 4 h.

steps.title: Churn and freeze
steps.text: Churn until thick and creamy, then pack into the container and freeze for at least 4 h.

tips: Use culinary-grade or better matcha; very cheap powder can taste bitter.
Grate the ginger on a fine grater so it gives up the most juice.
A common mistake is adding matcha to hot milk all at once, which leaves stubborn lumps; whisk it into cold milk first.
For more heat, steep the ginger for the full hour.
storage: Keep frozen in a covered container for up to 2 weeks. The green fades slightly with time and light, so an opaque container is best.
